fields.h1: Absolute Surrender by Andrew Murray: A Guide
fields.meta_title: Absolute Surrender by Andrew Murray: A Guide
fields.description: Andrew Murray’s classic presses one question: have you given yourself wholly to God? A guide to Absolute Surrender — its message, its themes, and how to read it.
fields.body_html:
Few small books have shaped the devotional life of the church as deeply as Andrew Murray’s Absolute Surrender. Written by the South African pastor and prayer-teacher whose gentle, searching books have guided believers into the deeper life for over a century, it presses a single, life-changing question: have you given yourself wholly and unreservedly to God? Murray’s answer is that the secret of a victorious Christian life is not more effort but complete surrender — laying down our own will and letting God have all of us. This guide walks through the book’s message, its key themes, and how to read it for the good of your own soul.

What the book is about

The heart of Absolute Surrender is captured in its opening illustration, drawn from an obscure Old Testament story. When a hostile king demanded that Israel’s king Ahab hand over everything — his silver, gold, wives, and children — Ahab consented. Murray seizes on this as a picture: “What Ben Hadad asked was absolute surrender; and what Ahab gave was what was asked of him — absolute surrender.” If a wicked king would yield everything to an enemy, how much more should we yield everything to a loving God?

That is the book’s thesis. God asks for all of us — not a portion, not the respectable parts, but the whole self, will and future included. And the wonderful discovery Murray presses is that this surrender is not a grim loss but the gateway to freedom, rest, and power. What we lay down, God takes up; what we surrender, he fills. The call echoes Paul’s great appeal: “present your bodies as a living sacrifice, holy and acceptable to God, which is your spiritual worship” (Romans 12:1).

The central message: God does the work

Murray’s most liberating insight is that surrender itself is God’s work in us, not merely our achievement. We may fear we cannot surrender fully — and we are right; we cannot, in our own strength. But Murray points to the promise that lifts the burden: “God is willing to work it in you.” Our part is to be willing and yielded; God’s part is to accomplish the surrender and to live his life through us. “It is God who works in you, both to will and to work for his good pleasure” (Philippians 2:13).

This rescues the book from becoming a heavy call to try harder. Murray is not urging us to squeeze out more willpower but to let go — to stop struggling to run our own lives and to hand the controls to God, trusting him to do in us what we cannot do ourselves. The surrendered life is therefore a restful life, lived by faith in the God who has promised, “he who calls you is faithful; he will surely do it” (1 Thessalonians 5:24).

Key themes to watch for

As you read, several threads recur. The first is the branch and the vine — Murray’s beloved picture of a life that bears fruit not by striving but by abiding, drawing everything from Christ as a branch draws sap from the vine (John 15). A branch’s whole business is simply to remain attached and let the life flow through; so is ours.

A second theme is the exchanged life — the truth Paul captured in “I have been crucified with Christ. It is no longer I who live, but Christ who lives in me” (Galatians 2:20). Surrender means the end of self-rule and the beginning of Christ’s rule within. A third is the Holy Spirit as the one who makes this real, filling and empowering the yielded believer. Throughout, Murray returns to the same note: God is more willing to possess us fully than we are to be possessed, and the whole of the Christian life is learning to let him.

What surrender is — and is not

It is worth clearing away two misunderstandings, because the word “surrender” can be misread. Surrender is not passivity — a limp doing-nothing that waits for God to move us like a puppet. Murray’s surrendered believers are among the most active in history; they simply act out of yieldedness rather than self-will, their energies now harnessed to God’s purposes instead of their own. Nor is surrender a single, once-for-all crisis that settles everything forever. It is a definite act, yes — but also a daily posture, renewed each morning, as fresh corners of the self come to light and are handed over in turn.

Understood rightly, surrender is the most reasonable thing in the world. Since Christ “died for all, that those who live might no longer live for themselves but for him who for their sake died and was raised” (2 Corinthians 5:15), to withhold ourselves from him is both ungrateful and self-defeating. And the paradox Murray delights to point out is that what feels like the greatest loss turns out to be the greatest gain. The surrendered life is not a diminished life but an enlarged one, freed at last from the exhausting tyranny of self.

The rest it leads to

The goal of surrender, for Murray, is rest. The believer who has stopped struggling to run their own life discovers the yoke Jesus promised: “Come to me, all who labor and are heavy laden, and I will give you rest... For my yoke is easy, and my burden is light” (Matthew 11:28–30). Much of our weariness comes from carrying what we were never meant to carry — the weight of managing our own sanctification, our own future, our own reputation. Surrender lays it all down at God’s feet and takes up his lighter yoke instead.

This is why Absolute Surrender, for all its searching demands, is finally a book about peace. It does not leave the reader burdened but relieved, having handed over to God what was crushing them. The surrendered heart can say with the Psalmist, “Return, O my soul, to your rest; for the Lord has dealt bountifully with you” — for it has found that the God who asks for everything gives back far more than he takes.

How to read it

Read Absolute Surrender slowly and prayerfully; it is not a book to rush. Each short chapter began as a spoken address, so it reads warmly, almost as if Murray were speaking to you personally. Take it a chapter at a time, pausing to let its searching questions do their work. Do not merely gather information — respond. When Murray asks whether you have surrendered a particular area, stop and actually surrender it.

It helps to read with a specific willingness: “Lord, whatever you show me is still mine and not yours, I will hand over.” The book is best used not as reading but as transaction — a place to meet God and give him what he asks. Many readers have found it wise to keep a pen nearby, writing out their own act of surrender when the moment comes. Approached this way, a short book becomes a turning point.

Why it still speaks today

More than a century after it was written, Absolute Surrender endures because it addresses the perennial problem of the divided heart — the Christian who wants God and self both, and finds neither joy nor power in the compromise. Murray’s answer is timeless because it is simply the gospel applied: the same Jesus who said “whoever would save his life will lose it, but whoever loses his life for my sake will save it” (Luke 9:24) still calls his followers to the paradox of surrender, where losing is finding and dying is living.

In an age even more crowded and self-absorbed than Murray’s, his call to yield everything to God is bracing and freeing. It cuts through our endless self-management and offers the rest of a life wholly given to a wholly trustworthy God. Read it, and let it ask you the one question it exists to ask: Will you surrender all? And let it answer, too, the fear that such surrender is too costly, by reminding you who is asking. We do not surrender to a tyrant who will exploit us, but to a Father who gave his own Son for us and can be trusted with everything we hand him. Nothing laid in those hands is ever lost.

Read it for yourself

The best way to profit from any guide is to go to the book itself, and Absolute Surrender rewards a first-hand reading. Come to it not as a critic but as a seeker, ready to meet God in its pages. And let it open the door to Murray’s wider world of devotional writing, for the same theme runs, like a golden thread, through everything he wrote — that the deepest secret of the Christian life is to give ourselves wholly to God and to let him be wholly our life. “Present yourselves to God as those who have been brought from death to life” (Romans 6:13), and discover, as generations of readers have, that in absolute surrender there is absolute rest.
